WITH counted AS (                     -- cancelled attempts do not exist for this report
  SELECT * FROM join_attempts WHERE outcome <> 'cancelled'
), marked AS (
  SELECT c.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER w AS rn,
         CASE WHEN LAG(attempt_ts) OVER w IS NULL
                OR attempt_ts - LAG(attempt_ts) OVER w > INTERVAL '120 seconds'
              THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS starts_try
  FROM counted c
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY meeting_id, user_id ORDER BY attempt_ts, attempt_id)
), tries AS (
  SELECT m.*,
         SUM(starts_try) OVER (PARTITION BY meeting_id, user_id
                               ORDER BY attempt_ts, attempt_id) AS try_no
  FROM marked m
), per_participant AS (
  SELECT meeting_id, user_id,
         MIN(tenant_id)                                                   AS tenant_id,
         MIN(client_platform) FILTER (WHERE rn = 1)                       AS client_platform,
         COALESCE(BOOL_OR(outcome = 'succeeded') FILTER (WHERE try_no = 1), false) AS first_ok,
         COALESCE(BOOL_OR(outcome = 'succeeded') FILTER (WHERE try_no > 1), false) AS later_ok
  FROM tries
  GROUP BY meeting_id, user_id
)
SELECT tenant_id, client_platform,
       COUNT(*)                                             AS participants,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT first_ok)                 AS failed_first_try,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT first_ok AND later_ok)    AS recovered_later,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT first_ok)::numeric / COUNT(*), 4) AS failed_share
FROM per_participant
GROUP BY tenant_id, client_platform
HAVING COUNT(*) >= {{min_participants}}
ORDER BY tenant_id, client_platform;

Explanation. A gaps-and-islands problem at the participant grain. Cancelled attempts are removed first (a no-op below Very Hard), so they can neither start nor bridge a try. Within each (meeting_id, user_id), ordered by attempt_ts, attempt_id, an attempt starts a new try when there is no previous attempt or the gap to the previous one is more than 120 seconds; a running SUM of that flag numbers the tries. One row per participant then carries the platform of row 1, whether try 1 contains a success and whether any later try does. BOOL_OR … FILTER returns NULL when no row matches, hence the COALESCE. The last step counts per tenant and platform and applies the floor in HAVING.

Complexity. One sort per participant partition for the two window functions (they share the window), then two hash aggregates: O(n log n) over attempts. In production the per-participant step would be computed once per meeting day and stored.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). Snowflake and BigQuery: the same LAG plus running SUM; booleans aggregate with BOOLOR_AGG (Snowflake) or LOGICAL_OR (BigQuery), and COUNT_IF/COUNTIF replace FILTER; timestamp differences use DATEDIFF('second', …) or TIMESTAMP_DIFF(…, SECOND). Spark SQL: lag, sum over a window, bool_or, count_if. MySQL 8: window functions are available; TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, …), SUM(CASE …) instead of FILTER, and MAX(outcome = 'succeeded') as the boolean aggregate. SQL Server: DATEDIFF(second, …), no FILTER, so SUM(CASE …).

Edge cases built into the data. Every level: a failure with a success 20–90 seconds later (not failed), a failure with a success 200–600 seconds later (failed and recovered), a failure with only failed retries. Hard: gaps of exactly 120 s (same try) and 121 s (new try); a chain of three attempts 100 s apart (one try, 200 s end to end); a failure on one platform and a quick success on another (counted on the first); two attempts in the same second on different platforms (the lower attempt_id is first); the same user in two meetings of one tenant. Very Hard: a cancelled attempt between a failure and a success 200 s apart (two tries once it is removed), a participant with only a cancelled attempt (not counted), a cancelled first attempt on another platform (the platform comes from the first counted attempt), and a floor that drops small groups.

Common mistakes. Measuring the first raw attempt instead of the first try; fixed time buckets (date_trunc) instead of gaps; measuring 120 s from the first attempt of the try rather than the previous attempt; < instead of <= at 120; grouping per user instead of per meeting and user; taking the platform of the successful or last attempt; MIN(client_platform) over all attempts (alphabetical, not first); leaving cancelled attempts in so they bridge two tries; forgetting COALESCE so NULL comparisons drop participants; integer division.

(2) Order by a server receive time or bound the skew; late attempts mean the day must be recomputed for a few days (or tries built over a trailing window), and the report says which days are still provisional. (3) Show counts with the share, add an interval (Wilson) or suppress groups under a minimum; compare with the tenant's own history rather than the global mean. (4) Carry each participant's open try (last attempt time and status) across batches as state, or reprocess a 120-second overlap at the batch edge; a try is final only once 120 s pass without an attempt.

WITH offered AS (                      -- the window starts at the device's FIRST offer
  SELECT device_id,
         MIN(offered_at)                              AS start_at,
         MIN(offered_at) + INTERVAL '{{days}} days'   AS end_at
  FROM update_offers
  WHERE update_id = '{{update_id}}'
  GROUP BY device_id
), status AS (
  SELECT o.device_id, d.ring,
         (SELECT b.os_build FROM device_builds b       -- build in effect at the first offer
           WHERE b.device_id = o.device_id AND b.effective_at <= o.start_at
           ORDER BY b.effective_at DESC LIMIT 1)      AS os_build,
         EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM update_installs i
                  WHERE i.device_id = o.device_id AND i.update_id = '{{update_id}}'
                    AND i.installed_at BETWEEN o.start_at AND o.end_at) AS compliant,
         EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM device_checkins c
                  WHERE c.device_id = o.device_id
                    AND c.checkin_at BETWEEN o.start_at AND o.end_at)   AS checked_in
  FROM offered o
  JOIN devices d ON d.device_id = o.device_id
)
SELECT ring, os_build,
       COUNT(*)                                               AS offered_devices,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE checked_in OR compliant)        AS online_devices,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE compliant)                      AS compliant_devices,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE compliant)::numeric
             / NULLIF(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE checked_in OR compliant), 0), 4) AS compliance_rate
FROM status
GROUP BY ring, os_build
ORDER BY ring, os_build;

Explanation. First reduce offers to one row per device that was offered this update, with the window anchored on the first offer (MIN), so re-offers cannot move it. Two EXISTS tests with inclusive BETWEEN decide compliance (an install of this update in the window) and whether the device checked in; a device is online if it checked in or is compliant, since an install proves it was on. The build is looked up as of the first offer with a correlated ORDER BY effective_at DESC LIMIT 1, which reads the history rather than devices.current_build. The aggregation keeps every offered device in offered_devices, and NULLIF turns an all-offline group's rate into NULL instead of an error or a misleading 0.

Complexity. One aggregate over offers, then per offered device three index-friendly probes (installs, check-ins, builds by device_id and time): O(d log n) with indexes on (device_id, time); without them, hash semi-joins over the three tables. Check-ins are by far the largest table in practice.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: no correlated LIMIT 1 subqueries in the select list on large tables; use a join and QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY effective_at DESC) = 1, TIMESTAMP_ADD(start_at, INTERVAL n DAY), SAFE_DIVIDE. Snowflake: an ASOF JOIN … MATCH_CONDITION (o.start_at >= b.effective_at) expresses the build lookup directly; DATEADD(day, n, start_at), DIV0NULL or NULLIF. Spark SQL: a range join on device and time plus row_number, date_add works on dates only, so use start_at + INTERVAL n DAYS. MySQL 8: LATERAL derived tables (8.0.14+) or a ROW_NUMBER join, DATE_ADD(start_at, INTERVAL n DAY).

Edge cases built into the data. Every level: an install exactly N days after the first offer (compliant), a device never online in the window (check-ins only before the offer or after the window), installs and offers of another update, devices never offered this update (some of which installed it anyway, and are not reported). Hard: re-offers, including an install inside the re-offer's window but after the first offer's; an install one second after the window; a compliant device with no check-in rows; a group whose only device was offline (NULL rate). Very Hard: build changes after the offer (current build differs) and a build change at exactly the offer time (it counts).

Common mistakes. Starting the window at the latest offer or at each offer; < instead of <= at the end of the window; counting installs of any update; dividing by offered devices (never-online devices count as failures); excluding a compliant device because it has no check-in; dropping the all-offline group or showing 0; grouping by current_build; joining check-ins and installs directly and counting rows.

(1) Generate day offsets 0..N, and for each offered device take the day of its first in-window install; cumulative counts over online devices give the curve (the online denominator is fixed by the whole window, or by day, which must be stated). (2) Model check-in gaps from devices with frequent heartbeats, or use other signals (update scans, sign-ins) as additional evidence of being online; report "unknown" separately rather than guessing. (3) Store pauses as intervals per ring and stretch the window by the paused time, or report "active days since offer"; either way the definition is versioned. (4) Precompute per device per day an "online" flag (or first/last check-in per day) incrementally; the report then joins offers to a small daily table instead of raw heartbeats; partition by day and cluster by device.

WITH last_accept AS (                  -- duplicates collapse; the clock runs from the last acceptance
  SELECT suggestion_id, MAX(event_ts) AS accepted_at
  FROM suggestion_events
  WHERE event_type = 'accepted'
  GROUP BY suggestion_id
), per_suggestion AS (
  SELECT s.app,
         COALESCE(s.language, 'und')     AS language,
         la.accepted_at IS NOT NULL      AS accepted,
         la.accepted_at IS NOT NULL
           AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM suggestion_events u
                            WHERE u.suggestion_id = s.suggestion_id
                              AND u.event_type = 'undone'
                              AND u.event_ts >  la.accepted_at
                              AND u.event_ts <= la.accepted_at + INTERVAL '5 minutes') AS kept
  FROM suggestions s
  LEFT JOIN last_accept la ON la.suggestion_id = s.suggestion_id
)
SELECT app, language,
       COUNT(*)                                  AS shown,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE accepted)          AS accepted,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE kept)              AS kept,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE accepted)::numeric / COUNT(*), 4) AS accept_rate,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE kept)::numeric
             / NULLIF(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE accepted), 0), 4)     AS keep_rate
FROM per_suggestion
GROUP BY app, language
HAVING COUNT(*) >= {{min_shown}}
ORDER BY app, language;

Explanation. The grain is the suggestion. All accepted events of a suggestion collapse to its last acceptance, which handles duplicate client events and re-acceptance after an undo at once. A suggestion is kept when no undone event falls in the half-open-on-the-left window (accepted_at, accepted_at + 5 minutes]: strictly after the last acceptance (an undo before it undid an earlier acceptance) and at most 300 seconds later. Starting from suggestions with a LEFT JOIN keeps suggestions with no events in shown; COALESCE(language, 'und') puts undetected languages in their own group; the floor is a HAVING on the per-suggestion count; NULLIF makes keep_rate NULL for a group with no acceptances.

Complexity. One aggregate over acceptance events, one anti-join probe per accepted suggestion (index on (suggestion_id, event_type, event_ts) or a hash semi-join), one aggregate: O(n log n) over events at worst.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: TIMESTAMP_ADD(accepted_at, INTERVAL 5 MINUTE), COUNTIF, SAFE_DIVIDE; NOT EXISTS with correlated subqueries is supported but a LEFT JOIN … WHERE u.suggestion_id IS NULL is the safer rewrite. Snowflake: DATEADD(minute, 5, accepted_at), COUNT_IF, DIV0NULL. Spark SQL: accepted_at + INTERVAL 5 MINUTES, a LEFT ANTI JOIN for the undo test, count_if. MySQL 8: accepted_at + INTERVAL 5 MINUTE, SUM(CASE …).

Edge cases built into the data. Every level: an undo exactly 300 s after the acceptance (not kept), an undo much later (kept), suggestions with no events, a language that appears only once or twice (below the floor). Hard: duplicate acceptance events, including one where the undo is 302 s after the first acceptance but 299 s after the last (not kept); undos at 299, 300 and 301 s; dismissed suggestions. Very Hard: accepted, undone, accepted again (kept if the second acceptance is not undone, not kept if it is); suggestions with no language, reported as 'und'.

Common mistakes. Counting acceptance events instead of suggestions; starting the clock at the first acceptance; an exclusive end (< 300); counting any undo, including one before the last acceptance; an inner join to events that drops suggestions with no events from shown; applying the floor to joined event rows or to accepted; dividing kept by shown; dropping or NULL-labelling suggestions without a language; integer division.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Compute, per suggestion, the first undo after the last acceptance (MIN(event_ts) FILTER (WHERE …)), then COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE first_undo IS NULL OR first_undo - accepted_at > INTERVAL 'k minutes') for each k. (2) Report keep rate only for clients known to log undo, or show coverage beside it; mixing clients biases apps whose clients do not log undo upward. (3) A floor on shown is not enough when one person dominates a group: add a minimum of distinct users, suppress complementary cells, or add noise; never expose per-user rows. (4) Emit the day after the last acceptance window closes (a watermark of 5 minutes plus lateness), mark late corrections as restatements, and keep a version of each published number.

from collections import deque


def match_lobby(players, max_gap):
    queues = {}
    for p in players:
        queues.setdefault(p[1], []).append(p)
    pairs, left = 0, []
    for region, ps in queues.items():
        gap = max_gap[region]
        ps.sort(key=lambda p: p[2])                  # by skill
        n = len(ps)
        skill = [p[2] for p in ps]
        wait = [p[3] for p in ps]
        # best[i]: (pairs, total matched wait) over the first i players, nobody half-paired.
        # A matched set can always be paired as consecutive members in skill order, so
        # player i either stays, or plays an earlier j with everyone between them left.
        best = [(0, 0)] * (n + 1)
        partner = [-1] * n
        window = deque()                             # (best[j] + (1, wait[j]), j), values decreasing
        for i in range(n):
            if i:
                j = i - 1
                v = (best[j][0] + 1, best[j][1] + wait[j])
                while window and window[-1][0] <= v:
                    window.pop()
                window.append((v, j))
            while window and skill[i] - skill[window[0][1]] > gap:
                window.popleft()
            stay = best[i]
            if window:
                (k, w), j = window[0]
                play = (k, w + wait[i])
                if play > stay:
                    best[i + 1] = play
                    partner[i] = j
                    continue
            best[i + 1] = stay
        pairs += best[n][0]
        i = n
        while i:                                     # walk the choices back
            j = partner[i - 1]
            if j >= 0:                               # i - 1 played j; those between waited
                left.extend(p[0] for p in ps[j + 1:i - 1])
                i = j
            else:
                left.append(ps[i - 1][0])
                i -= 1
    left.sort()
    return pairs, left

Explanation. Regions are independent. Within a region, sort by skill. Any set of players that some pairing covers can be paired as consecutive members in skill order: if a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ d are paired as (a, c), (b, d) or (a, d), (b, c), then (a, b) and (c, d) are within the gap too. So, scanning in skill order, player i either stays or plays an earlier player j with everyone between them staying, and best[i + 1] = max(best[i], best[j] + (1, wait[j] + wait[i])) over the j with skill[i] - skill[j] <= gap. The value best[j] + (1, wait[j]) of a candidate j is fixed once computed and the valid j form a window whose left edge only moves right, so a deque that keeps values decreasing gives the window maximum in O(1) amortised. Tuples compare as "pairs, then wait". Walking the recorded choices back from the end lists the players who stayed. The answer is unique because the player sets that some pairing covers form a matroid (the matching matroid); its bases all have the maximum number of pairs, and with distinct waits the maximum-weight basis is unique.

Complexity. O(n log n) for the sort and O(n) for the pass and the walk back; O(n) memory. The timing test (150 001 players, skills over 2 000 values, gap 25, so about 2 000 players inside each gap) runs in about 0.6–0.8 s in CPython. The same DP that scans every earlier player in the gap (O(n·w)) did not finish in 60 s; pair search over all pairs is O(n²) and worse.

Dialect notes. Java: sort an index array by skill, ArrayDeque<int[]> for the window, values as long pairs compared manually. C++: std::deque and std::pair<int, long long>, whose operator< is lexicographic. In SQL, a pairing like this is sequential and does not express well; a Spark job would group by region and run the DP per group. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A gap of exactly max_gap (paired) and of max_gap + 1 (not); an empty lobby; one player; four players where pairing the longest waiter with their closest opponent strands both ends (two pairs exist); three in a chain where either end can be left (the shorter waiter stays). Hard: a chain of five where pairing from the lowest skill leaves the wrong player; max_gap 0 with equal skills; three equal skills (the shortest waiter stays). Very Hard: equal skills in different regions (never paired), and regions with different gaps.

Common mistakes. Greedy pairing of neighbours from the lowest skill (right count, wrong players left); pairing the longest waiter first with their nearest opponent (loses pairs); maximising total wait without putting the pair count first (it happens to coincide here because waits are positive, but the candidate should say why); < instead of <= for the gap; forgetting to add the players skipped between j and i when walking back; mixing regions; an O(n·w) scan of the window per player.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Neighbour greedy is optimal for the count by an exchange argument (the lowest player can always be paired with the next one if with anyone), but it ignores waits, so among equally many pairs it may leave a long waiter; the DP fixes that. (2) With per-player gaps (|a - b| <= max(g_a, g_b) or min), compatibility is no longer an interval relation on one line, the uncrossing argument fails and the problem becomes general matching on an interval-like graph; practical systems widen gaps in steps and rerun the snapshot. (3) Pre-form groups, treat each group as one item with an average skill and pair groups the same way; mixing group sizes makes it a harder assignment. (4) Track how many snapshots each player has missed, include it in the wait, and alert on a long tail of waits per skill band; the extremes of the skill range are where starvation shows up first.

Rubric anchors. 2: right count but wrong players left, or an O(n·w) or O(n²) solution. 3: passes everything with the sorted DP and a window maximum. 4: also justifies the uncrossing step and the uniqueness of the answer, and discusses widening gaps and starvation.

Strong signals. Separates "how many pairs" from "who waits" before coding; proves the adjacency claim on a four-player example. Red flags. Claiming a greedy is optimal without an argument; general matching libraries for a one-dimensional problem.

def scan(signatures, chunks):
    # Build the trie: goto[s] maps a byte to the next state, out[s] lists
    # (length, sig_id) for every signature that ends in state s.
    goto, fail, out = [{}], [0], [()]
    for sig_id, pattern in signatures:
        s = 0
        for b in pattern:
            nxt = goto[s].get(b)
            if nxt is None:
                nxt = len(goto)
                goto[s][b] = nxt
                goto.append({})
                fail.append(0)
                out.append(())
            s = nxt
        out[s] = out[s] + ((len(pattern), sig_id),)
    # Failure links breadth-first; merge each node's outputs with its failure
    # node's, so a state reports every signature that is a suffix of its string.
    queue = deque(goto[0].values())
    while queue:
        s = queue.popleft()
        for b, t in goto[s].items():
            queue.append(t)
            f = fail[s]
            while f and b not in goto[f]:
                f = fail[f]
            g = goto[f].get(b, 0)
            fail[t] = g if g != t else 0
            if out[fail[t]]:
                out[t] = out[t] + out[fail[t]]

    found = []

            s = goto[s].get(b, 0)

def cheapest_tiering(reads, tiers):
    SHIFT = 20                       # key = cost << SHIFT | changes: one comparison orders both
    INF = 1 << 200
    spec = []
    for name in tiers:
        t = tiers[name]
        cap = max(t["min_days"], 1)  # days in the tier, counted up to the minimum
        early = [max(0, t["min_days"] - k) * t["store"] << SHIFT for k in range(1, cap + 1)]
        spec.append((t["store"], t["read"], cap, early, t["enter"] << SHIFT, t["leave"] << SHIFT))
    # cur[i][k - 1]: cheapest key for the days so far, ending in tier i after k days there
    cur = []
    for store, read, cap, early, enter, leave in spec:
        row = [INF] * cap
        if read is not None or reads[0] == 0:
            row[0] = (store + reads[0] * (read or 0)) << SHIFT
        cur.append(row)
    for r in reads[1:]:
        # the cheapest way to end a stay in each tier yesterday: shortfall plus leave fee
        out = [min(map(int.__add__, row, sp[3])) + sp[5] for row, sp in zip(cur, spec)]
        nxt = []
        for i, (store, read, cap, early, enter, leave) in enumerate(spec):
            if read is None and r > 0:          # offline tier on a day with reads
                nxt.append([INF] * cap)
                continue
            day = (store + r * (read or 0)) << SHIFT
            move_in = min(o for j, o in enumerate(out) if j != i) + enter + 1
            row = cur[i]
            if cap == 1:
                new = [min(row[0], move_in) + day]
            else:
                new = [move_in + day]
                new.extend(v + day for v in row[:-2])
                new.append(min(row[-2], row[-1]) + day)   # at or past the minimum
            nxt.append(new)
        cur = nxt
    # deletion after the last day: the final stay's shortfall, no leave fee

def _fmt(ts, offset_min):
    return datetime.fromtimestamp(ts + offset_min * 60, timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")


def attendance_report(meeting, events):
    first, sessions, open_at = {}, {}, {}
    for ev in events:
        key = ev["user"] or "guest:" + ev["name"]           # guests keyed by name
        device = (key, ev["device"])
        if ev["type"] == "join":
            first.setdefault(key, ev["ts"])                  # the first join survives a rejoin
            open_at[device] = ev["ts"]
        elif device in open_at:
            sessions.setdefault(key, []).append((open_at.pop(device), ev["ts"]))
    for (key, _), start in open_at.items():                  # still connected when the meeting ended
        sessions.setdefault(key, []).append((start, meeting["end"]))
    report = {}
    off = meeting["tz_offset_min"]
    for key, spans in sessions.items():
        spans.sort()
        total, run_start, run_end = 0, None, None            # union of sessions on absolute time
        for start, end in spans:
            if run_end is None or start > run_end:
                if run_end is not None:
                    total += run_end - run_start
                run_start, run_end = start, end
            elif end > run_end:
                run_end = end
        total += run_end - run_start
        report[key] = {

Common mistakes. Fixing the double count by taking last_leave − first_join, which counts the gap of a rejoin; merging intervals that are in clock time, so the midnight bug survives; subtracting the offset instead of adding it; using datetime.fromtimestamp(ts) without a zone, which depends on the machine's local time; keying guests by device; rewriting the whole function instead of making minimal fixes.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Keep open sessions in state and compute the union with "now" as the provisional end. Recompute incrementally per attendee. (2) Buffer per meeting until a watermark, sort by timestamp, and make first join a min. Pairing joins and leaves needs order per device, so use a per-device sequence number if clocks disagree. (3) Use the scheduled length if the meeting ended on time, and the actual length if it overran, and state the choice in the report. The union already handles several devices. (4) Pseudonymise guests per meeting, for example "Guest 3", with a mapping held only for the organiser if the tenant allows it.

Rubric anchors. 2: finds two or three bugs; several checks still fail. 3: all five fixed, every check passes, each one explained. 4: also explains why arithmetic and formatting must be separated, adds a regression test per bug, and gives good answers on live reports and late events.

Strong signals. Reproduces each complaint with a three-event case before changing code; notices that the two-device check was built so bug 1 cannot mask it. Red flags. Clamping negative durations to zero; "convert everything to local time first".

MSF-L2-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Event schema as an allow-list. event_id, tenant_id, user_object_id, app, action_type (enum), outcome (enum), client_version, ts_utc. The ingestion edge validates against the schema and drops every unknown field before anything is written. Free-text fields are rejected by type: enums and ids only. Error queues store the validated envelope and the reason, never the raw body. Service logs at the edge log ids and reasons only. A content scanner samples the stored data for long strings or prompt-like text and alerts.
  • Ingestion. Events land per region in the tenant's geography, partitioned by tenant_id and UTC date. Deduplicate by event_id within a window covering client retries (for example 48 hours), with a later daily dedup pass over the partition.
  • Per-user daily activity. One row per (tenant, user, app, day) with action counts by type and an active flag (at least one intentional action). This table is small compared with events, and it is the base for everything else.
  • Exact distinct users per period. A per-user summary (tenant, user, app, last_active_day, active_days_bitmap_180), or simply the daily activity table queried with COUNT(DISTINCT user) over the period's days per tenant, which is exact and cheap at tenant scale. Daily distinct counts are never summed. Report snapshots are materialised daily for 7, 30, 90 and 180 days.
  • Licences. A daily snapshot of licence assignments from the directory export, kept as validity intervals per user. Adoption = active licensed users ÷ licensed users on the period's last day (state the choice), with unlicensed activity reported separately.
  • Concealment and identity. Storage holds the directory object id. Concealment is applied when serving: a per-tenant keyed hash (HMAC with a tenant-specific secret) gives stable pseudonyms within the tenant that cannot be linked across tenants. Names are joined from the directory at serving time, so they disappear when the user does.
  • Small groups. Department breakdowns show counts only for groups of at least {{min_group}} users. Smaller groups are merged into "Other", and complementary suppression ensures a hidden cell cannot be recovered by subtracting from totals.
  • Deletion. A directory deletion feed drives deletion of the user's rows from the activity tables and materialised reports within 30 days; aggregates keep counts but no identifier. A deletion log proves completion.
  • Residency and isolation. Pipelines run per geography; only tenant-level aggregates with no user identifiers may leave a region, and only if policy allows. Every query is scoped by tenant_id, enforced by the serving layer.
  • Definitions and restatement. Metric definitions are versioned. A definition change recomputes from the per-user daily table (events are not needed), the report shows the definition version and a note, and history is restated for the visible window.

Competing designs to accept. A streaming pipeline with per-tenant state for today and a batch job for history; a warehouse with dbt-style models over the daily activity table; HyperLogLog sketches for cross-tenant or exploratory views, provided tenant-facing active-user counts stay exact. Each is fine if content never lands and deletion is complete.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. A free-text field slipping through a deny-list; error queues, crash dumps or debug logs holding raw payloads; summing daily active users; pseudonyms that are global hashes; suppression that can be undone by subtraction; deletion that misses materialised snapshots; very large tenants making per-tenant partitions skewed; directory sync failures making licence denominators wrong.

Incident guidance.

  • An error field carries prompt fragments in about 0.1% of {{daily_actions}} events: the allow-list should have dropped the field at the edge. If it did not, stop ingestion of that field, identify the affected partitions by scanning for the field, purge them (rebuild from the dropped-field version), purge error queues and logs, and record what was deleted and when. Treat it as a privacy incident with the owners of the client release, and add a schema test that fails on any free-text field.
  • A directory sync failure marks users in 300 tenants as unlicensed: detect it with a monitor on day-over-day licence changes per tenant. Hold the report refresh for affected tenants, keep yesterday's licence snapshot, re-run once the export is fixed, and annotate the day if a report was already published.
  • A department below {{min_group}} users can be derived by subtraction: apply complementary suppression or merge small groups into "Other" before totals are shown, and audit published reports for the same pattern.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Detection by a content scanner and schema monitoring; deletion by partition rebuild, plus logs and queues; prevention by the allow-list and a release check. (2) Suppress the group and a complementary one, or merge it into "Other". (3) Recompute from the per-user daily table under the new definition, show the version, and restate within the window. (4) Move per-user data with the tenant under a migration plan; until complete, reports read from the old region; nothing per-user is duplicated across regions. (5) Publish only aggregates across many tenants (for example percentiles of adoption by size band, each band with enough tenants), never anything that identifies a tenant.

Rubric anchors. 2: stores raw events "temporarily", sums daily active users, global hashes for pseudonyms. 3: allow-listed schema, per-user daily table with exact distinct counts, serving-time concealment, suppression, deletion and residency covered. 4: also closes the error-queue and log leaks, prevents subtraction attacks, versions metric definitions with restatements, and gives concrete incident plans.

Strong signals. Starts with the event schema and what is not in it; asks how admins will compare numbers with licences. Red flags. "We hash the prompt so it is safe"; approximations for tenant-facing counts with no explanation.

MSF-L2-05.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Landing. Activity events land raw and immutable, partitioned by event date, deduplicated by event_id (a started and a succeeded event are different events of one operation, linked by an operation or correlation id). Listings land as immutable snapshots with the read time of each resource, not just the listing's start.
  • Identity. resource_key is a surrogate. resource_id_history(resource_key, resource_id_normalised, display_id, valid_from, valid_to) maps every id string a resource has had to its key, compared case-insensitively. A move or rename event closes the old id's interval and opens the new one on the same key. If a listing shows a new id with the same type, name and properties as a resource that vanished, a heuristic link can be proposed but is marked inferred.
  • From events to state. Succeeded create and update events mark a resource as changed at a time. Properties come from a read of the resource shortly after (a targeted read queue), or from the next listing. A delete closes the current version. A resource group delete closes every resource whose id is under that group at that time.
  • History model. resource_versions(resource_key, valid_from, valid_to, type, location, resource_group, subscription, sku, tags, source observed|inferred, caller, event_id), as validity intervals. Late events are inserted by splitting the interval they fall in. When a listing contradicts the current version, an inferred version starts at the listing's read time for that resource (the honest bound), with the earlier bound recorded as "changed between t1 and t2".
  • Reconciliation. After each listing ({{listing}}): resources in the listing but not in state get an inferred create; resources in state but not in the listing, and not changed during the listing window, get an inferred delete; property differences become inferred updates. Reconciliation is skipped for subscriptions whose listing failed.
  • Daily inventory. A view or materialised table: versions valid at the end of each UTC day. Because history is append-and-split and inputs are versioned, any past day can be recomputed and gives the same answer for the same inputs. Corrections from late events are visible as restatements with a change log.
  • Outputs. Inventory by day for finance (joined to cost by resource_key through the id-history table, so cost follows moves); change history with caller and source for security and audit; data quality metrics (inferred change share, event lag, listing coverage).

Competing designs to accept. Rebuild-from-snapshots only, with events as a supplement for timing and caller (accept if the candidate explains the lost changes between listings); an event-sourced store replayed into state with periodic snapshot checkpoints; a lakehouse with SCD2 MERGE. Any is fine if identity survives moves and inferred changes are labelled.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Using the id string as the primary key; trusting events as complete; treating a listing as an instant; overwrite-only state; case-sensitive joins; cascade deletes missed; event bursts from policies overwhelming targeted reads; the activity log's {{log_retention}} retention expiring during an outage.

Incident guidance.

  • The event feed stalls for six hours: alert on event lag. The next listing infers the missed changes with no caller and a time range. When the feed recovers, backfill the stalled events (within {{log_retention}}) and upgrade inferred changes to observed ones where an event matches, adding the caller. Tell security which changes remain without a caller.
  • 400 resource groups move overnight and cost allocation drops by a third: cost is joined by the new ids, which are not yet linked to their resource keys. Link them from the move events (old id to new id), and fall back to inferred links from the listing. Rerun the allocation for the affected days, and add a monitor on unallocated cost share.
  • A tagging policy rewrites a tag across {{subscriptions}} subscriptions in an hour: the targeted read queue would explode. Rate-limit reads, coalesce updates per resource, and let the next listing fill in properties. The history records one inferred or observed version per resource with the policy as caller.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Inferred creates with valid_from at the read time and an "earliest possible" bound unknown, flagged as found by listing. (2) Close every resource under that group at the delete time, with source observed for the group and inferred for its contents. (3) Join cost through the id-history table to the resource key, so both ids map to one resource. (4) Rebuild from the oldest listing available plus the events still retained; mark the gap as unknown; never invent a change time. (5) Show the caller as recorded (a policy or service identity), with the policy assignment if it can be found.

Rubric anchors. 2: an overwrite-only current-state table keyed by id; events trusted as complete. 3: surrogate keys with id history, validity-interval history, reconciliation against listings, observed vs inferred changes. 4: also honest timestamps for inferred changes, late-event interval splitting, cascade deletes, cost joins across moves, and concrete incident plans.

Strong signals. Asks what an event actually contains before designing; treats the listing as a series of reads, not an instant. Red flags. "The resource id is the key"; filling inferred changes with the listing's start time without saying so.

MSF-L3-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Series. meeting_series (series_id, organiser_id, tenant_id, title, tz_name, rrule, dtstart_local, until_local NULL, created_at, superseded_by_series_id NULL, split_from_series_id NULL, split_at_original_start NULL). The rule and its start are stored in the organiser's wall-clock time with an IANA zone name, never as a UTC offset. Edits to the series as a whole are versions: meeting_series_version (series_id, version, rrule, dtstart_local, tz_name, valid_from, valid_to), so "what the series said last month" is a lookup.
  • Occurrence identity. occurrence_key = (series_id, original_start_local) — the iCalendar RECURRENCE-ID idea. It is derived from the rule, so it exists before the occurrence is materialised and it never changes when the occurrence moves. A single meeting is a series of one.
  • Exceptions. series_exception (series_id, original_start_local, kind modified|cancelled, new_start_utc NULL, new_end_utc NULL, attendee_delta, recorded_at, version) — append-only; the latest version per key wins.
  • Materialised occurrences. occurrence (occurrence_id = hash(series_id, original_start_local), series_id, original_start_local, scheduled_start_utc, scheduled_end_utc, status scheduled|moved|cancelled, materialised_at). Expanded per occurrence from the rule using the zone database at expansion time, for a rolling {{horizon_months}}-month horizon, plus the past. Exceptions are applied as they arrive (an upsert of one occurrence), not only on a nightly rebuild. A time-zone database update re-expands future occurrences of affected zones.
  • "This and following". Ends the old series with until_local just before the split point and creates a new series with split_from_series_id and split_at_original_start. Past occurrences keep their keys; future ones of the old series are marked superseded (or simply no longer generated). A series_lineage view links the halves for yearly reports.
  • Attendance. participant_session (session_id, join_link_id, participant_id or guest marker, joined_at, left_at, client, received_at), deduplicated on session_id (at least once). Attribution, written as its own table session_occurrence (session_id, occurrence_id, rule_version, matched_how): the occurrence of that join link whose [scheduled_start − grace_before, scheduled_end + grace_after) contains joined_at; if two match, the one whose scheduled start is nearest; if none, unmatched (an ad-hoc use of the link), never silently dropped. A session that runs across two occurrences' windows stays with the occurrence it joined (or is split by time — either, if stated).
  • Recordings and transcripts. Attached by the meeting service to the online meeting instance at recording start, then mapped to the occurrence by the same rule; store the mapping and its method.
  • Facts. fct_occurrence (one row per occurrence: series, organiser, status, scheduled minutes, invitees, attendees, minutes attended, no-show flag for one-to-ones); fct_participant_occurrence (one row per person per occurrence: attended minutes, joined late, left early); fct_person_day_meeting_hours. Cancelled occurrences have no expected attendees and no no-show.

Competing designs to accept. Storing only the rule and exceptions and expanding at query time (fine for a calendar UI; expensive for warehouse reporting at {{daily_occurrences}} a day, so a materialised past is still needed). Event sourcing of calendar changes with occurrences as a projection. Keying occurrences by a service-issued instance id, if it is stable under moves and recoverable for future instances. Splitting a long session across occurrences by time instead of assigning it to one.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Occurrence keys built from the actual start (moves re-key); expansion with fixed UTC offsets (wrong for half the year); nightly-only exception application; "this and following" implemented as an edit of the original series (re-keys the past); infinite series fully materialised; attendance attributed by date only (two occurrences on one day); guests and duplicate sessions inflating attendance; tz database updates ignored.

Incident guidance.

  • DST week: occurrences an hour off, joins unmatched, no-shows doubled: the series had been expanded once with a fixed UTC offset. Contain by labelling the week's no-show metric and re-expanding future occurrences from the stored zone name; correct the past by re-expanding affected occurrences and re-running attribution for the week (the unmatched sessions are kept, so this is possible). Guard: store tz_name, never an offset; a test that expands a series across a DST change in {{dst_regions}}; alert when the unmatched-session share jumps.
  • "This and following" re-keyed two years of occurrences: the edit changed the original series' rule in place and occurrence ids were derived from the new rule. Contain by restoring the previous series version's occurrences from history; fix by implementing the split (old series ended, new series linked) so past keys never change; re-point attendance and recordings by the old keys; guard with a check that the number of past occurrences of a series never changes after an edit.
  • Late cancellations shown as 100% no-show: exceptions were applied only at the nightly rebuild of the next {{horizon_months}} months. Apply each exception as it arrives (upsert one occurrence), recompute affected facts, exclude cancelled occurrences from no-show denominators, and add a freshness check comparing exception events with occurrence status.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Stored: rule in local time with zone; expanded: each occurrence converted with that zone's rules, so the UTC start moves by an hour and attendees elsewhere see the meeting shift during the weeks when the two regions' clocks change on different dates. (2) One modified exception (Tuesday → Wednesday) on the old series; old series ended before the split; new series of Thursdays starting the week after; the moved occurrence keeps its key. (3) A stated rule: nearest scheduled start, or the occurrence in progress at join time; record matched_how. (4) Rolling horizon extended daily; beyond it, "meeting hours next quarter" is computed from rules (expand on demand) and labelled as a projection. (5) Occurrences partitioned by scheduled date, clustered by series; a late exception touches one occurrence and the facts for its date.

Rubric anchors. 2: one meetings table with a start time; moves create new meetings; UTC offsets. 3: series, exceptions and occurrences separated; stable key from original start; zone name stored; an attribution rule for shared links. 4: also the split with linked lineage, incremental exception application, a horizon strategy, at-least-once dedup, unmatched sessions kept, and the three incidents traced to these choices.

Strong signals. Brings up RECURRENCE-ID or original start unprompted; asks how joins are attributed when the link is shared. Red flags. "Store everything in UTC" for a recurring rule; materialising forever; deleting a cancelled occurrence.

MSF-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Identity. device (device_key surrogate, tenant_id, created_at), device_id_map (device_id, device_key, valid_from, valid_to) and device_hardware (device_key, hardware_id, valid_from, valid_to). A re-registration with the same hardware id in the same tenant maps the new device id to the existing device_key; a move to another tenant (resale) creates a new device_key, so history never crosses tenants. Renames are attributes with history, not identity.
  • Rings. ring (ring_id, tenant_id, name), ring_settings_version (ring_id, quality_deferral_days, feature_deferral_days, paused, valid_from, valid_to, changed_by, reason), and device_ring_assignment (device_key, ring_id, valid_from, valid_to) — both versioned (type 2 intervals).
  • Build catalogue. os_build (build_id, version, build_number, revision, update_type quality|feature, released_at, supersedes_build_id) with a total order (version, build, revision) so "on or after the latest quality build" is a comparison. Quality updates are cumulative, so a device is current if its build ≥ the latest released revision for its version.
  • Offers and attempts. update_offer (offer_id, device_key, build_id, ring_id, ring_settings_version, offered_at) — the offer records the settings version it was made under. install_attempt (attempt_id, offer_id, device_key, build_id, started_at) and install_state_event (event_id, attempt_id, state, error_code NULL, device_time, device_seq, received_at) with a legal transition graph (offered → downloading → downloaded → installing → pending_restart → installed | failed; installed → removed). Events deduplicated by event_id; ordered by device_seq when present, else by the transition graph, never by device_time alone.
  • Observed state. heartbeat (device_key, build_id, device_time, received_at) (sampled daily at full grain for weeks, then compacted).
  • Derived build history. device_build_interval (device_key, build_id, valid_from, valid_to, source event|heartbeat|both, confidence): built from installed/removed events, confirmed or corrected by heartbeats (a heartbeat from a later received time showing a different build closes the interval). Rollbacks produce a new interval on the previous build — the build can go down.
  • Facts. fct_attempt (one row per attempt: offer → installed duration, final state, error code, rollback flag); fct_device_day (daily snapshot: ring, build, online flag, is_current) for ring coverage; failure rate by build and error code over attempts.
  • Definition. "Share of ring on latest build N days after release" = devices in the ring (as of that day) seen online in the last 28 days whose build interval on that day is ≥ the latest released build, ÷ those devices; offline devices reported separately.

Competing designs to accept. A current-state table plus an append-only change log (if history is rebuilt from the log). Event sourcing per device. A daily device snapshot as the main history (coarser, but acceptable if intra-day rollbacks are captured in attempts). Hardware-id-first identity, if resale across tenants is handled.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Current-build columns overwritten (no as-of); trusting install events without considering removals; trusting device clocks for order or for partitioning; reimage creating a new device; ring settings stored only as current; offline devices counted as failures; heartbeat storage at {{devices}} devices a day.

Incident guidance.

  • Rolled-back devices still counted on the new build: "installed" was terminal in the model. Contain by deriving builds from intervals that close on a removed event or a contradicting heartbeat; recompute the dashboard for the month; guard with a reconciliation between the dashboard's build share and the heartbeat build share per build, alerting when they diverge by more than about {{rollback_share}}.
  • Deferral shortened, earlier offers flagged late: ring settings were not versioned. Backfill settings history from the admin audit log, store the settings version on every offer, and judge timeliness against that version; add a test that changing settings does not change past compliance.
  • Mass reimage made the fleet grow and histories restart: identity was the device id. Map the new device ids to existing device keys through hardware id within the same tenant, merge histories, recompute ring coverage, and add a monitor on new-device registrations per tenant per day.

Follow-up guidance. (1) The transition graph; a later state wins only if it is reachable; duplicates are no-ops; out-of-order arrivals are placed by device_seq. (2) Intervals: old build → new build (installed) → old build (removed) → new build (reinstalled); the week counts the device as current only on days its interval is the latest build. (3) Same tenant and hardware id: history joined; new tenant: not joined, and the old tenant's history is not visible to the new owner. (4) The offer carries the settings version; early relative to the old deferral but on time under the new one, with the change's author and reason. (5) Events and attempts kept at full grain for a release cycle or two; heartbeats compacted into intervals; daily device snapshots for trend reports.

Rubric anchors. 2: a devices table with a current build and status. 3: attempts with state events, ring assignment history, a derived build history, a stated "latest" definition. 4: also identity across reimage and resale, versioned ring settings tied to offers, rollback-aware intervals reconciled with heartbeats, clock-skew handling, and storage tiers.

Strong signals. Asks how a rollback is reported and which clock orders events. Red flags. Ordering by device timestamp only; counting offline devices as failed; one row per device updated in place.

MSF-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Tree with validity. mg_node (mg_id, tenant_id, name), mg_parent (mg_id, parent_mg_id, valid_from, valid_to) (adjacency, versioned), and a derived mg_closure (ancestor_id, descendant_id, depth, valid_from, valid_to) rebuilt for the affected subtree on each change (the tree is small: at most {{mg_depth}} levels). Subscriptions are leaves: subscription_placement (subscription_id, mg_id, valid_from, valid_to).
  • Lower levels. resource_group (rg_key, subscription_id, name, created_at, deleted_at). resource (resource_key surrogate, type, created_at, deleted_at) and resource_id_history (resource_id_path, resource_key, rg_key, subscription_id, valid_from, valid_to): a move closes one id path and opens another for the same key. Resolution of move pairs comes from the move activity event (source and target ids); the daily snapshot confirms.
  • Tags as rows. tag_assignment (scope_type sub|rg|resource, scope_key, tag_name_normalised, tag_name_original, tag_value, valid_from, valid_to, set_by). A rewrite with the same value does not open a new row (change compaction). Names compared case-insensitively and values case-sensitively in this exercise.
  • Effective tags. A derived effective_tag_day (resource_key, day, tag_name, tag_value, source resource|rg|subscription) using the stated precedence — or computed at query time for the questions that need it. The rule is documented, because the platform does not inherit tags itself in this exercise.
  • Rollups. Cost facts keyed by resource_key and usage date (the resource id path is kept for audit). Usage-date allocation: join cost to resource_id_history → subscription → subscription_placement → mg_closure, all valid on the usage date. Current-structure view: the same join with today's intervals. Invoiced months are frozen in a chargeback_statement table; a later change shows as a restatement line, never as a silent rewrite.
  • Policy scope as of D. Descendants of the assignment's scope in mg_closure valid on D → subscriptions → resource groups → resources alive on D.
  • Corrections. When the snapshot shows a change the events missed, write the interval with valid_from = the snapshot time (or the best known time from the activity log), flagged source=snapshot, and publish a correction event so downstream rollups for the affected dates recompute.

Competing designs to accept. Materialised path strings with validity instead of a closure table. A daily snapshot of the whole hierarchy (simple, and at a few thousand to a million subscriptions per day it is affordable; tags per resource per day are the expensive part). Tags as a JSON map with type 2 rows per resource, if names are normalised and no-op rewrites are compacted.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Recursive walks per row per day; joining cost to today's hierarchy for past months; resource id as the key across moves; tag columns per name; case-variant tag names split; tag churn from automation; missed events never reconciled.

Incident guidance.

  • Mid-month subscription move re-allocated a whole invoiced month: the report joined to the current tree. Contain by restoring the frozen statement for the invoiced month; switch the chargeback to usage-date allocation through intervals; show the move as a restatement in the next month if finance wants it; guard with a check that a closed month's totals per department never change on a rebuild.
  • Tag remediation rewrote every tag; history tripled; churn spiked: no-op rewrites were recorded as changes. Compact consecutive rows with the same normalised name and value; recompute "tag changes per day" from real value changes, which should return to about {{tag_change_share}}; guard with change compaction at write time and an alert on churn far above its baseline.
  • Moved resources split into deleted plus new: identity was the id path. Pair the old and new ids from the move events, map both to one resource_key, re-attribute cost history, and add a test that every move event yields exactly one key with two id intervals.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Closure rows for the moved group's subtree close on the 15th and reopen under the new ancestors; usage-date allocation splits the month at the 15th, current-structure gives the whole month to the new department. (2) One resource key, two id intervals, cost split by usage date between the subscriptions (and departments) it was in. (3) Effective tag on D = the resource's own interval valid on D, else the resource group's, else the subscription's; untagged before the 20th under usage-date rules, re-labelled only in an explicitly "as today" report. (4) Compaction of no-op rewrites and storing intervals, not daily rows. (5) Interval written from the snapshot with its source, a correction event, and recomputation of affected dates.

Rubric anchors. 2: parent ids with recursive queries against the current tree; tags as columns; resource id as the key. 3: versioned tree (closure or path) with as-of rollups; tags as rows with history; a stable resource key. 4: also both allocation rules with frozen invoiced months, a precedence rule with case handling, change compaction, snapshot reconciliation, and policy scope as of a date.

Strong signals. Separates "as of usage date" from "as of today" before being asked; proposes a closure table with validity. Red flags. Rebuilding history from the current tree; treating a move as delete plus create in cost reports.

MSF-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Catalogue. title (title_id), product (product_id, title_id, kind base|edition|add_on, requires_product_id NULL, platforms). Edition upgrades and add-ons depend on a base right.
  • Immutable sources. licence_grant (grant_id, player_id, product_id, source purchase|redemption|bundle|member_discount, order_id, granted_at, platform_scope, region, subscription_id NULL); licence_revocation (grant_id, revoked_at, reason refund|chargeback|fraud); subscription_period (player_id, subscription_id, tier, valid_from, valid_to, reason paid|grace|lapsed|resumed); catalogue_window (title_id, tier, platform, region, joins_at, leaves_at, announced_at) — windows are closed by setting leaves_at, never deleted; sharing_membership (group_id, owner_id, member_id, valid_from, valid_to).
  • Derived access intervals. access_interval (player_id, product_id, right owned|subscription|shared, source_id, platform, region, valid_from, valid_to): owned = grant to revocation; subscription = intersection of the player's paid periods with the title's catalogue windows for their tier, platform and region; shared = owner's owned interval ∩ membership interval, ending when the owner's licence ends (refund) or the membership ends. Add-ons are playable only where a base right overlaps. Rebuilt per player from sources (deterministic), so any past date can be answered and corrections are recomputations.
  • Precedence. One stated rule, e.g. owned > shared > subscription (or owned > subscription > shared, if the publisher model wants it). Session attribution writes session_right (session_id, player_id, product_id, right, source_id, rule_version) — exactly one row per session, deduplicated by session id; a session is attributed using the rights valid at its start (and, if it runs past a leave time, by the platform's stated rule).
  • Reports. Hours by title and right per month from session_right; publisher statements for closed months frozen, with later corrections (refund-related) as restatement lines in the next period.

Competing designs to accept. Answering "could they play on D" directly from sources at query time (correct and fine for support, too slow for monthly play attribution at {{players}} players). An entitlement event log with a state projection per player. Precedence by "the right that costs the platform least" if stated and stable.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Current-only entitlement tables; deleting catalogue rows; boolean "owns" flags; double attribution when two rights overlap; refunds not propagated to shared rights; time zones on leave dates; add-ons playable without a base; interval explosion (players × catalogue titles) — subscription intervals can be stored per player-period and joined with catalogue windows at query time instead of being exploded per title.

Incident guidance.

  • Deleted catalogue rows broke "could they play last month" and changed a closed month: deletion destroyed a source. Restore windows from backups or the catalogue's change history with leaves_at set; make windows append-only; freeze closed publisher months so rebuilds cannot change them; add a test that a rebuild of a closed month reproduces its frozen totals.
  • Member-discount buyers double counted in their last {{leave_notice_days}} days: sessions joined to every matching right. Enforce one row per session with the precedence rule; recompute the affected months and publish restatements; add a uniqueness constraint on session id in the attribution table and a check that attributed hours equal played hours.
  • Refund left a family's shared intervals open: shared intervals were not derived from the owner's licence end. Rebuild shared intervals as intersections, close them at the refund time for all {{family_size}} members, re-attribute play after the refund (not before), and add a check that no shared interval outlives its source grant.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Subscription interval until purchase; owned interval from the purchase; with owned > subscription, sessions after the purchase count as owned; the subscription interval ends at the leave date regardless. (2) Owner's licence and every derived shared interval close at the refund time; hours before the refund keep their attribution; the closed month is restated only if the platform's rule requires it. (3) Leave time defined per region (local midnight or a UTC instant, stated); a session that started before is allowed to finish or is cut — stated, and attributed by its start. (4) Tier history as periods; the support view lists, per day, the tier and the catalogue windows that applied. (5) Owned and shared intervals materialised; subscription access computed as period × window at query time; partitions by player hash; refresh per player on source change.

Rubric anchors. 2: an entitlements table of (player, title) with a flag. 3: rights as intervals derived from immutable sources, subscription access as an intersection, a precedence rule. 4: also add-on dependencies, refunds propagating to shared rights from the right time, one right per session with dedup, regional leave times, frozen publisher months, and an interval-size strategy.

Strong signals. Asks "which right" before "could they"; keeps catalogue windows forever. Red flags. Deleting rows when titles leave; attributing a session to several rights; treating a refund as if the purchase never happened (rewriting past play).

MSF-L3-05.html:
Reference solution (PostgreSQL; {{start_day}} and {{end_day}} are the instance's first and last reported days)

WITH days AS (
  SELECT g::date AS day, g + INTERVAL '1 day' AS day_end
  FROM generate_series(TIMESTAMPTZ '{{start_day}} 00:00:00+00',
                       TIMESTAMPTZ '{{end_day}} 00:00:00+00',
                       INTERVAL '1 day') AS g
), ev AS (                                       -- each evaluation with the lifetime it falls in
  SELECT e.evaluation_id, e.policy_id, e.resource_id, e.evaluated_at, e.compliance_state,
         r.created_at, r.deleted_at
  FROM policy_evaluations e
  JOIN resources r
    ON r.resource_id = e.resource_id
   AND e.evaluated_at >= r.created_at
   AND (r.deleted_at IS NULL OR e.evaluated_at < r.deleted_at)
), latest AS (                                   -- latest evaluation per day, policy and lifetime
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (d.day, ev.policy_id, ev.resource_id, ev.created_at)
         d.day, d.day_end, ev.policy_id, ev.compliance_state, ev.deleted_at
  FROM days d
  JOIN ev ON ev.evaluated_at < d.day_end
  ORDER BY d.day, ev.policy_id, ev.resource_id, ev.created_at,
           ev.evaluated_at DESC, ev.evaluation_id DESC
)
SELECT day, policy_id,
       COUNT(*) AS assessed_resources,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE compliance_state = 'compliant') AS compliant,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE compliance_state = 'non_compliant') AS non_compliant,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE compliance_state = 'compliant') / COUNT(*), 1) AS compliance_pct
FROM latest
WHERE compliance_state <> 'exempt'
  AND (deleted_at IS NULL OR deleted_at >= day_end)
GROUP BY day, policy_id
ORDER BY day, policy_id;

Explanation. The calendar comes from generate_series, so days with no new evaluations still get rows. Each day is joined to every evaluation made before its end (half-open: evaluated_at < day_end), and DISTINCT ON keeps the latest per day, policy and resource lifetime — that is the carry-forward. Ties on evaluated_at go to the larger evaluation_id; ids are otherwise not in time order, so they never decide "latest" alone. The exempt filter and the existence check come after the latest row is chosen: an exempt latest state hides an earlier non-compliant one, and a resource deleted before the day's end leaves the report although its last evaluation is still the latest. Joining evaluations to resources on the lifetime that contains them makes the same query correct at every level: at Medium and Hard each resource has one lifetime; at Very Hard a re-created resource's evaluations from the earlier lifetime belong to the deleted row and never reach the new one.

Complexity. Days × evaluations before each day's end, then a sort for DISTINCT ON: O(D · E log E) for D days. Fine for a report window; at production volume the daily trend comes from a state-change interval table (resource, policy, state, valid_from, valid_to) joined to the calendar, or from a daily snapshot built incrementally from yesterday's snapshot plus today's evaluations.

Dialect notes. DISTINCT ON is PostgreSQL; Snowflake, BigQuery and Databricks SQL use QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY day, policy_id, resource_id, created_at ORDER BY evaluated_at DESC, evaluation_id DESC) = 1 (MySQL 8 and Spark without QUALIFY: a subquery on the row number). Calendars: GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY + UNNEST (BigQuery), GENERATOR / ARRAY_GENERATE_RANGE or a date dimension (Snowflake), sequence() + explode (Spark). COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …) becomes COUNT_IF (Snowflake, BigQuery COUNTIF, Spark count_if) or SUM(CASE …). Rounding of exact halves can differ for floating-point types: keep the division in NUMERIC/DECIMAL. None of these variants is executed here.

Edge cases built into the data. Resources evaluated days before the first reported day (carried in); an evaluation exactly at midnight that flips a state (belongs to the new day); a resource deleted exactly at midnight (counted the day before, gone from that day); a resource deleted in the middle of a day (gone from that day); resources created mid-range and evaluated hours or a day later; a policy that applies to only some resources; evaluation ids in random order; evaluations after the last day. Hard adds exempt as a latest state hiding a non-compliant one and two evaluations of one resource and policy at the same instant with different states. Very Hard adds a resource deleted and re-created with the same id, with a day on which the new lifetime exists but has not been evaluated.

Common mistakes. Counting only each day's evaluations (no carry-forward); counting every evaluation instead of the latest; ignoring deleted_at; deleted_at > day_end (drops a resource deleted exactly at midnight a day early); evaluated_at <= day_end (counts a midnight evaluation in the previous day); latest per resource across policies; latest by MAX(evaluation_id); (Hard+) filtering exempt rows before choosing the latest; tie broken the wrong way; (Very Hard) joining evaluations on resource_id alone, which carries the earlier lifetime's state into the re-created resource (or duplicates rows). Each has a diagnostic. A window function over the whole table without the day in the partition returns today's state for every day.

Follow-up guidance. (1) A state-change interval table built by comparing each evaluation with the previous one per resource and policy (LAG), closed by deletion; the daily trend is an interval-to-calendar join; correctness checked by recomputing a sample of days from raw evaluations. (2) LAG(compliance_state) per resource and policy ordered by evaluated_at, evaluation_id; count rows where it differs (first evaluation counted as a change or not — stated). (3) Exempt resources, resources never evaluated and deleted ones are outside the denominator; a good dashboard shows the not-yet-evaluated count beside the percentage. (4) Add state_age = day_end − evaluated_at and flag beyond the scan interval; whether stale states count is a policy choice, but they should be visible.

Rubric anchors. 2: latest evaluation per resource overall, or only the day's evaluations. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains the interval table or incremental snapshot, real state changes with LAG, and what the denominator leaves out.

Strong signals. Builds the calendar first; asks whether deleted resources and exempt states count before writing. Red flags. MAX(evaluation_id) as "latest"; grouping by evaluated_at::date and calling it a daily trend; ignoring deletions.
